titel: How US funds and ETFs are taxed
kurz: Why US mutual funds and ETFs pay out their income every year, how a fund distribution is split into qualified dividends, ordinary dividends and capital gain distributions, and why foreign funds are a tax trap for US investors.

bloecke.md:
A US mutual fund or ETF is usually organized as a regulated investment company (RIC) under Subchapter M of the Internal Revenue Code (26 U.S.C. §§ 851–855). A RIC pays no corporate income tax on the income it passes on to its shareholders. To keep this status, it must distribute at least 90% of its net investment income every year, and to avoid a 4% excise tax (§ 4982), it distributes practically all of its income and net realized gains.

The consequence is simple: there are no accumulating funds in the US in the tax sense. Every fund distributes, and you owe tax on the distributions in the year they are paid, even if they are automatically reinvested. What differs from fund to fund is not whether income is taxed, but what kind of income is distributed and how much of it there is.

## What a distribution consists of

After the end of the year, the fund tells you on Form 1099-DIV how its distributions are to be treated. The fund passes through the character of its own income:

- **Ordinary dividends** (box 1a) include interest from bonds, short-term gains and dividends that do not meet the conditions for qualified dividends. They are taxed at ordinary rates.
- **Qualified dividends** (box 1b) are the part of box 1a that stems from qualified dividends of the companies held. They are taxed at 0%, 15% or 20%, provided you held the fund shares for more than 60 days around the ex-dividend date.
- **Capital gain distributions** (box 2a) pass on the fund's net long-term gains. They are taxed as long-term gains no matter how long you have held the fund shares.
- **Section 199A dividends** (box 5) pass on REIT dividends. They are ordinary dividends, but you can generally deduct 20% of them.
- **Nondividend distributions** (box 3) are a return of capital. They are not taxed now but reduce your basis.
- **Foreign tax paid** (box 7) can be claimed as a credit or deduction.

Interest from municipal bond funds is passed through as exempt-interest dividends and is free of federal income tax.

bloecke.md:
**Buying a distribution.** Mutual funds typically pay capital gain distributions in December. If you buy just before the record date, the share price falls by the distribution, and you owe tax on what is economically a return of your own money. Many funds publish estimates of their year-end distributions in the autumn.

**Short holding periods.** If you sell fund shares held for six months or less at a loss after receiving a capital gain distribution, the loss is treated as long-term up to the amount of that distribution (§ 852(b)(4)). Qualified dividend treatment also fails if you did not hold the fund shares for more than 60 days around the ex-dividend date.

**Commodity and currency products.** Many commodity ETFs are partnerships that issue a Schedule K-1 instead of a Form 1099, and physically backed gold and silver trusts are taxed as collectibles at up to 28%. These products are not RICs and follow their own rules.

## Why ETFs rarely distribute capital gains

When investors sell shares of a mutual fund, the fund often has to sell securities to pay them, and the gains it realizes are distributed to all remaining shareholders. An ETF works differently. Large market participants create and redeem ETF shares by exchanging them for baskets of the underlying securities. When an ETF hands out securities in such an in-kind redemption, it does not recognize a gain (§ 852(b)(6)). The ETF can deliberately give away the lots with the lowest basis.

As a result, many broad stock index ETFs have not paid any capital gain distributions for many years, while actively managed mutual funds in taxable accounts often distribute several percent of their value. Dividends are passed through by both. For a long-term investor in a taxable account, this difference is one of the most important tax advantages of ETFs.

## Tax drag

Because distributions are taxed every year, a fund in a taxable account grows somewhat more slowly than the same fund in an IRA or 401(k). This loss is called tax drag. It depends on how much the fund distributes and how the distribution is taxed, not on how well the fund performs.

bloecke.beispiel: A stock index ETF with a 1.3% yield, 95% qualified and no capital gain distributions, at 15% and 22%: 1.3% × (0.95 × 15% + 0.05 × 22%) = 0.20% a year.

bloecke.md:
You hold $30,000 in a taxable account and are in the 22% bracket and the 15% range for long-term gains. The yields are assumptions for illustration.

- **Stock index ETF:** 1.3% dividends = $390.00, of which 95% are qualified. Tax: $370.50 × 15% + $19.50 × 22% = $55.58 + $4.29 = $59.87, or 0.20% of the value.
- **Actively managed stock mutual fund:** 1.0% qualified dividends = $300.00 and a capital gain distribution of 4% = $1,200.00. Tax: $300 × 15% + $1,200 × 15% = $225.00, or 0.75% of the value.

The active fund costs $165.13 more tax in this year, before any difference in fees, and you pay it even though you sold nothing and the money was reinvested.

## Reinvested distributions raise your basis

A distribution that is reinvested buys new fund shares. You have already paid tax on it, so it becomes part of your basis. When you sell, your gain is the sale price minus all purchases including the reinvested distributions. Brokers track this for shares bought since 2012 and report the basis on Form 1099-B. For older shares, or after transfers between brokers, you have to check it yourself. Leaving out reinvested distributions means paying tax twice on the same money.

You buy fund shares in 2026 for $30,000 and sell them in 2031 for $50,000. Over the five years, distributions of $2,500 were paid and reinvested, all taxed at 15%. This figure is an assumption.

| Step | Amount |
|---|---|
| Sale price | $50,000.00 |
| Basis: purchase plus reinvested distributions | −$32,500.00 |
| Long-term gain | $17,500.00 |
| Tax on sale (15%) | $2,625.00 |
| Already paid on distributions ($2,500 × 15%) | $375.00 |
| Total | $3,000.00 |

Without distributions, the gain would have been $20,000 and the tax $3,000, the same amount. If you forget the reinvested distributions in your basis, you report $20,000 of gain and pay $375 too much.

The kind of income a fund distributes determines how much tax you pay; the distributions themselves determine when you pay it. Reinvested distributions are part of your basis and must not be taxed a second time when you sell.

## Foreign funds and the PFIC rules

For US investors, funds domiciled outside the US are a tax trap. Almost every non-US fund, including the UCITS ETFs domiciled in Ireland or Luxembourg that are popular in Europe, is a passive foreign investment company (PFIC) under 26 U.S.C. § 1297: at least 75% of its income is passive or at least 50% of its assets produce passive income. The [[Fund domicile|domicile]] matters, not the index or the currency.

Under the default rules of § 1291, a gain on the sale of PFIC shares and any distribution above 125% of the average of the prior three years are excess distributions. They are spread evenly over your holding period. The part allocated to earlier years is taxed at the highest ordinary rate that applied in each of those years, currently 37%, plus interest as if the tax had been paid late. The preferential rates for long-term gains never apply. An accumulating fund makes this worse, because the entire return is concentrated in one large excess distribution when you sell.

There are two elections that soften this. A qualified electing fund (QEF) election taxes your share of the fund's income each year at normal rates, but it requires an annual information statement from the fund that most European funds do not provide. A mark-to-market election taxes the increase in value each year as ordinary income. Either way, you generally have to file Form 8621 for each PFIC every year.

bloecke.titel: Federal tax on a $10,000 gain after 10 years: US ETF versus foreign fund
bloecke.unter: Simplified illustration. US ETF: long-term gain at 15%. PFIC with mark-to-market election: annual increases taxed as ordinary income at an assumed 24%. PFIC default rules: gain spread evenly over 10 years, nine prior years at 37% with interest approximated at 7% a year, current year at 24%.

bloecke.md:
Distributions are taxable even if every cent is reinvested, and nothing is withheld for US investors. If your funds pay large capital gain distributions in December, the tax is due with your January estimated payment or your return in April. Keep enough cash outside the fund, or set your estimated payments accordingly.

With PFICs, it can be worse: under a mark-to-market election, you owe tax on increases in value every year although the fund pays out nothing.

bloecke.titel: If you moved to the US with European funds
bloecke.md:
If you become a US tax resident, for example with a green card or under the substantial presence test, your existing UCITS ETFs and other non-US funds become PFIC holdings from then on. A savings plan into such funds should normally not be continued. Several reporting duties also apply: the FBAR (FinCEN Form 114) if your foreign accounts together exceed $10,000 at any time in the year, and Form 8938 if your specified foreign financial assets exceed $50,000 at the end of the year or $75,000 at any time (single filers living in the US; twice that for joint filers).

Whether it is better to sell the funds before the move, to keep them under an election or to sell them after the move depends on the tax rules of both countries, the size of the gains and the planned length of stay. The tax treaty between the two countries does not remove the PFIC rules. This is a case for advice from a professional who knows both systems.

1. In a taxable account, prefer US-domiciled ETFs with low turnover. Broad index ETFs rarely distribute capital gains.
2. Use asset location: hold tax-inefficient funds such as bond funds, REIT funds and actively managed funds in a 401(k) or IRA if you have room there.
3. Before buying a mutual fund in November or December, check the fund's estimated year-end distribution and its record date.
4. Keep your basis current when distributions are reinvested, and do not buy non-US funds in a US taxable account.

mitnehmen: US funds and ETFs are regulated investment companies that distribute practically all income and net gains every year; there are no accumulating funds in the tax sense.
Form 1099-DIV splits a distribution into qualified dividends, ordinary dividends, capital gain distributions, Section 199A dividends and return of capital, each taxed differently.
Capital gain distributions are long-term no matter how long you held the fund; ETFs rarely make them because in-kind redemptions remove gains without tax.
Reinvested distributions add to your basis, so the total tax over the holding period stays the same; only the timing changes.
Non-US funds such as UCITS ETFs are PFICs for US investors, with punitive default taxation, annual Form 8621 filings and no access to long-term rates.

begriffe.text: Fund that meets the requirements of 26 U.S.C. §§ 851–855 and pays no corporate tax on income it distributes. It must distribute at least 90% of its net investment income and in practice distributes nearly everything.
Distribution of a fund's net long-term capital gains, reported in box 2a of Form 1099-DIV. It is taxed as a long-term gain regardless of how long the investor has held the fund shares.
Part of a fund distribution that stems from REIT dividends, reported in box 5 of Form 1099-DIV. It is taxed as ordinary income, but 20% of it can generally be deducted.

Non-US company or fund with at least 75% passive income or at least 50% passive assets (26 U.S.C. § 1297). US investors are taxed under punitive default rules unless they make a QEF or mark-to-market election, and generally must file Form 8621 every year.

Redemption of ETF shares by handing over securities instead of cash. The fund does not recognize a gain on the securities it hands out (26 U.S.C. § 852(b)(6)), which is why ETFs rarely distribute capital gains.
